By the fundamental theorem of algebra, write
\[
p(z)=c\prod_{k=1}^{m}(z-\lambda_k),\qquad c\ne0,
\]
where the roots are listed with multiplicity.

If $p$ has $m$ distinct roots, then each root has multiplicity one. Fix a root $\lambda_j$ and write $p(z)=(z-\lambda_j)q(z)$, where $q(\lambda_j)\ne0$. Differentiating gives
\[
p'(z)=q(z)+(z-\lambda_j)q'(z),
\]
so $p'(\lambda_j)=q(\lambda_j)\ne0$. Thus $p$ and $p'$ have no root in common.

Conversely, if $p$ does not have $m$ distinct roots, then some root $\lambda$ has multiplicity $n\ge2$. Hence $p(z)=(z-\lambda)^nq(z)$ with $q(\lambda)\ne0$. Differentiating,
\[
p'(z)=n(z-\lambda)^{n-1}q(z)+(z-\lambda)^nq'(z),
\]
so $p'(\lambda)=0$. Therefore $\lambda$ is a common root of $p$ and $p'$. This proves the equivalence.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Factor $p$ over $\mathbf C$, counting multiplicities:
\[
p(z)=c\prod_{k=1}^m(z-\lambda_k),\quad c\ne0.
\]
The roots of $p$ are distinct exactly when every root has multiplicity one.

Assume first that all roots are distinct. For any root $\lambda$, write $p(z)=(z-\lambda)q(z)$ with $q(\lambda)\ne0$. Then
\[
p'(z)=q(z)+(z-\lambda)q'(z),
\]
and hence $p'(\lambda)=q(\lambda)\ne0$. Thus no root of $p$ is a root of $p'$.

For the reverse implication, suppose $p$ and $p'$ have no common root. If $p$ had a repeated root $\lambda$, then for some $n\ge2$ we could write
\[
p(z)=(z-\lambda)^nq(z),\quad q(\lambda)\ne0.
\]
Differentiation yields
\[
p'(z)=n(z-\lambda)^{n-1}q(z)+(z-\lambda)^nq'(z),
\]
so $p'(\lambda)=0$, contradicting the absence of a common root. Therefore every root is simple, and since $\deg p=m$, $p$ has $m$ distinct roots.
\end{proof}

p(z)=c\prod_{i=1}^r(z-\alpha_i)^{n_i},

\[
p'(\alpha_i)=q_i(\alpha_i)\ne0.
\]
Consequently, if all $n_i=1$, $p$ and $p'$ have no common root.

\[
p(z)=(z-\alpha_i)^{n_i}q_i(z),
\qquad q_i(\alpha_i)\ne0.
\]
Therefore
\[
p'(z)=n_i(z-\alpha_i)^{n_i-1}q_i(z)+(z-\alpha_i)^{n_i}q_i'(z),
\]
which implies $p'(\alpha_i)=0$. Since also $p(\alpha_i)=0$, the two polynomials have a common root. Hence the absence of common roots forces every $n_i=1$, so $p$ has $m$ distinct roots.
\end{proof}

\begin{proof}
Factor $p$ over $\mathbf C$ with distinct roots $\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_r$ and multiplicities $n_1,\ldots,n_r$:
\[
p(z)=c\prod_{i=1}^r(z-\alpha_i)^{n_i},
\qquad c\ne0,
\qquad \sum_{i=1}^r n_i=m.
\]
Thus $p$ has $m$ distinct roots precisely when $r=m$, equivalently when every $n_i=1$.

Suppose first that every $n_i=1$. For each $i$, write $p(z)=(z-\alpha_i)q_i(z)$, where $q_i(\alpha_i)\ne0$. Then
\[
p'(z)=q_i(z)+(z-\alpha_i)q_i'(z),
\]
so $p'(\alpha_i)=q_i(\alpha_i)\ne0$. Hence no root of $p$ is a root of $p'$.

Conversely, suppose $p$ and $p'$ have no common root. If some multiplicity $n_i$ were at least $2$, then differentiating
\[
p(z)=(z-\alpha_i)^{n_i}q_i(z)
\]
would give
\[
p'(z)=n_i(z-\alpha_i)^{n_i-1}q_i(z)+(z-\alpha_i)^{n_i}q_i'(z),
\]
so $p'(\alpha_i)=0$. This contradicts the hypothesis, since $p(\alpha_i)=0$ as well. Therefore all $n_i=1$, and consequently $r=m$; hence $p$ has $m$ distinct roots.
\end{proof}
